comments.why_zh: 这场演示展示的概念领先于其所处的时代数十年。
comments.quote_zh: 如果你还没看过，那一个小时的四十多分钟绝对值得花。
comments.text_zh: 我刚刚在听 Douglas Crockford 的一场演讲，里面谈到了 Engelbart 对计算机科学做出的贡献。真正让我印象深刻的，是他在那次演示中展现出的新概念数量之多——那场演示虽然做于 1968 年，却展示出了此后几十年都未曾出现的特性，其中一些至今仍未得到有效应用。如果你还没看过，那一个小时的四十多分钟绝对值得花。我也觉得，此刻正适合反思一下：能参与这样一门仍处于极早期阶段的科学，是多么不可思议——它发展史上的奠基性人物如今依然健在、安好。让我们不要忘记他们的贡献，更重要的是，不要忽视那些若在今天采用、就能让我们远远超越现状的概念。Douglas Engelbart 的“所有演示之母”：[VIDEO]
comments.text: I was just listening to one of Douglas Crockford's talks which discussed the contributions Engelbart made to computer science. What really stuck with me was the sheer number of new concepts he showed in his demo, which, though made in 1968, would showcase features not seen for decades, and some of which are still not effectively in use. If you haven't seen it, it's well worth the hour and forty minutes. I think this is also a good moment to reflect on how incredible it is to be involved in a science which is still so much in its infancy that seminal figures in its development are still alive and well. Let us not forget their contributions, and most importantly, not overlook the concepts that, if employed today, can advance us far beyond where we are now. Douglas Engelbart's Mother of All Demos: [VIDEO]

I've put the out-the-box backend CMS in front of people that interact with computers very little and they instantly "get it". All data is simply a node in a hierarchy, and is easily movable and editable. I don't understand why more frameworks don't copy this basic structure. If you watch "The mother of all demos"[1] the structure is almost visually 95% the same. I look at Angular and it's looks complicated - the article is about how complicated it is. comments.text_zh: TempleOS 有些地方其实让我想起 MOAD[1]，甚至有点像 Acme[2] 编辑器。纯文本的美妙之处在于解释起来非常简单（Unicode 就未必了）。换成别的东西，你就得开始担心向前/向后兼容、字节序等等……不过我想，如果你只需要考虑一个平台，大概会容易些。我喜欢那个索引的概念。已经有过不止一次（成功的）努力去构建完全支持内容索引的文件系统，但它们通常是隐式索引。通过文件内容做显式索引也许挺有意思。我不太确定把所有东西都跑在 Ring-0 的真正理由是什么。我想不出多少理由能说明超出最小权限会有什么好处。[1] [VIDEO] [2] [LINK]
comments.text: Some of TempleOS actually reminded me of the MOAD[1], and even the Acme[2] editor a bit. The beauty of plain text is that it's trivial to interpret though (not unicode so much). Anything else and you need to start to worry about backward/forward compatibility, byte orders, etc... I imagine it's probably easier when you only have only one platform to think about though. I liked the index concept. There have been more than one (successful) efforts to build a filesystem that fully supports indexing content, but they're generally implicit indexes. Explicit indexing via file content might be interesting. I'm not sure what the real justification for running everything in Ring-0 is. I can't think of many reasons for anything more than minimal privileges to be a benefit. [1] [VIDEO] [2] [LINK]

comments.author: partycoder
comments.story_title: What made Xerox PARC special? Who else today is like them?
comments.why_zh: Engelbart 1968 年的演示作为 PARC 的背景。
comments.text_zh: 施乐曾经是一家利润极其丰厚的企业。它是复印机市场的先行者，并长期保持很大的市场份额。在帕洛阿尔托研究中心（PARC），他们拥有合适的团队、合适的想法，研究也完全是朝着正确的方向推进。比如，他们有曾参与 Douglas Engelbart 的“oN-Line-System”的前 SRI International 研究员，该系统于 1968 年展示，也就是如今所称的“所有演示之母”（[VIDEO]，[LINK]）。他们的成果包括创造了出色的 Xerox Alto 计算机系统，配有 GUI 和作为输入设备的鼠标，这启发了 Apple Macintosh 和 MS Windows（这段故事被多次搬上银幕，尤其是经典的《硅谷海盗》）。施乐的领导层没能看清像 Alto 这样的创新如何转化为有利可图的产品……即便在今天看来这似乎不言自明。那是一次千载难逢的机会，他们放走了，结果其他公司大量从 PARC 的成果中获利，至今依然如此。此外，复印机已不再处于商业活动的中心，纸张使用量也在下降。这让施乐成了一家属于过去的公司，就像 Kodak 或 Blockbuster（无意冒犯，但这么说很公道）。
comments.text: Xerox was an immensely profitable business once. Being first to market with photocopiers, and keeping a large market share for a long time. In the Palo Alto Research Center (PARC), they had the right team, the right ideas and research was absolutely going in the right direction. For instance, they had former SRI International researchers that participated in the Douglas Engelbart's "oN-Line-System", presented in 1968 in what is now known as "the mother of all demos" ( [VIDEO] , [LINK] ). Their achievements include the creation of the excellent Xerox Alto computer system featuring a GUI and a mouse as input device, which inspired the Apple Macintosh and MS Windows (a story dramatized in multiple occasions, notably in the classic "Pirates of Silicon Valley"). Xerox leadership failed to visualize how innovations like the Alto could be converted into profitable products... even if it looks self-evident today. That's a once in a lifetime opportunity that they let go and as a result other companies heavily profited from PARC's findings and continue to do so today. In addition, photocopiers are no longer at the center of business activities, and usage paper is decreasing. This makes Xerox a company of the past, like Kodak or Blockbuster (not trying to be offensive, but it is fair to say so).

comments.text: > human-machine cooperation is probably where the big money will be. As it has been for as long as machines have existed, really. This reminds me of Douglas Engelbart and his vision for computers. I'll cite the section of his wikipedia page that paraphrases an interview with him from 2002[0][1]. > [Douglas Engelbart] reasoned that because the complexity of the world's problems was increasing, and that any effort to improve the world would require the coordination of groups of people, the most effective way to solve problems was to augment human intelligence and develop ways of building collective intelligence. He believed that the computer, which was at the time thought of only as a tool for automation, would be an essential tool for future knowledge workers to solve such problems. He was right of course, and his work lead to "The Mother of All Demos"[1]. Machine learning is the next step in using computers as thought enhancement tools. What we still need to figure out is an appropriate interface that is not as "black-boxy" as "we trained a neural net, and now we can put X in and get Y out". EDIT: Now that I read that quoted section of wikipedia again, it's funny to note that computers were "only seen as tools of automation", and how modern fears of AI are also about automation. Automation of thinking. [0] [LINK] [1] [LINK] [2] [VIDEO]

comments.author: kkfx
comments.story_title: Qubes OS: A reasonably secure operating system
comments.why_zh: GUI 和视频会议早于 Unix 的例子。
comments.text_zh: 好吧，和历史上前辈系统相比，Unix 是另一个非常糟糕的操作系统：一开始，他们决定用一种糟糕的编程语言来减少对硬件性能的需求，并把这种廉价语言与用户语言分开（C 用于系统、用于“复杂”的事情，shell 脚本用于最终用户）；出于同样的理由，他们决定不需要 GUI，而在 Unix 之前很久，我们就已经有了 GUI、触摸显示器，甚至在局域网里做过世界上第一次带屏幕共享的视频会议（也就是所谓的“所有演示之母”，1968 年 [1]）。后来他们意识到那也没那么好，图形系统开始出现在 Unix 上，但非常受限、复杂，完全违背了 Unix 原则，因为对于 GUI 来说并没有 IPC；经典的 PostScript GUI 确实支持某种用户编程，但并不真正像经典系统那样；CDE 支持一定程度的集成，但同样没法和经典系统相比。从那以后，所有“现代”系统都在以有限、有限且充满 bug 的方式，重新发现历史系统几十年前就做得更好的东西……我觉得很多人应该看看像 [LINK] 这样的经典广告，然后看看它的日期和今天的我们……这不只是安全问题，而是整体设计。过去硬件资源有限，所以各种 hack 和缓慢很常见，硬件本身处于“开拓阶段”，充满了 hack 和丑陋之处，但如果继续演化那些系统，我们本可以登上月球，而我们现在仍在中世纪…… [1] [VIDEO]
comments.text: Well, unix is another really bad OS compared to it's historical predecessors: at first they decide for a bad programming language to need less hw horsepower and separate that cheap language from the user language (C for the system, for "complex" things, shell scripts for the end user), for equal reasons they decide that's no need for GUIs, while far before unix we have had GUIs, touch monitor, even the world first video-conference with screen sharing in LAN (the so called Mother of all the Demos, in 1968 [1] then they realize that's was not that good and graphic systems start to appear on Unix, far limited, complex, that completely violate unix principles since for GUIs there were no IPCs, classic PostScript GUIs do support some user-programming but not really something like classic systems, CDE support a certain integration but again nothing like classic systems. Since them all "modern" systems keep rediscovering in limited, limited and bug ridden ways what historical systems have done far better decades before... I think many should just see classic advertisement like [LINK] than see it's date and where we are today... It's not only security it's the overall design. In the past hw resources was limited an so hacks and slowness were common, hw itself being "in a pioneering phase" was full of hacks and ugliness but evolving those systems would have led us too the moon while we are still in the middle age... [1] [VIDEO]

comments.author: kps
comments.story_title: No_color
comments.why_zh: 展示了 NLS 使用类似的显示风格。
comments.text_zh: Engelbart 的 NLS 也是如此，正如在“所有演示之母”中看到的那样。[VIDEO] 现有为数不多的实际研究表明，对于视力正常的人，浅底深字更易读。白内障患者受益于深底浅字，而散光患者受益于浅底深字。
comments.text: As did Engelbart's NLS, as seen in ‘the mother of all demos’. [VIDEO] What little actual research exists suggests dark on light is more readable for people with normal vision. People with cataracts benefit from light on dark, and people with astigmatism benefit from dark on light.

comments.author: ralferoo
comments.story_title: Igneous Linearizer: semi-structured source code
comments.why_zh: 旧的研究想法值得重新审视。
comments.quote_zh: 我时不时会重看 1968 年的"The Mother of All Demos"[1]
comments.text_zh: 我记得 2000 年代初读过一篇关于 Source Code In Database 的文章，从那以后它就一直在我的脑子里打转，每隔几年我就会琢磨一下。我就是摆脱不了一种感觉：这里藏着一种未来范式的种子，到那时所有人都会想"为什么我们以前不一直这么做？"，但每次我试着把这些想法推到结论，总感觉那不过是在重新实现 Smalltalk，然后问题就变成"为什么 Smalltalk 没有更流行？"。话虽如此，重新审视旧想法还是很有价值的。60 年代和 70 年代在各种五花八门的方向上做过那么多有趣的研究，也许是因为当时对于事情该怎么做还没有先例或预期。这里未开发的资源多得离谱。我时不时会重看 1968 年 Douglas Englebert 演示斯坦福部分研究的"The Mother of All Demos"[1]，或者 1963 年 Ivan Sutherland 展示基于 GUI 的 CAD 系统的 Sketchpad Demo[2]。幸运的是，这些想法现在又被捡起来了，但对我来说有趣的是，从这些想法出现到成为主流，中间隔了多么长的时间。其中一部分原因显然是成本，因为最先进的研究机器比甚至二十年后的家用电脑还要强大得多，但我确信有很多好想法就是被遗忘了。我认为，部分问题在于，我们已经……
comments.text: I remember reading an article on Source Code In Database back in the early 2000s, and it's been knocking around my brain ever since as something I ponder every couple of years. I just can't shake the feeling that there's the gem of a future paradigm where everyone wonders "why we didn't always do it that way?", but then every time I try to follow those thoughts through to a conclusion, it always feels like it'd just be re-implementing Smalltalk, and then the question is "why isn't Smalltalk more popular?" That said, there's a lot to be said for revisiting old ideas. There was so much interesting research done in the 60s and 70s in all sorts of random directions, maybe because at that time there were no precedents or expectations for how things should be done. There are so many untapped resources here, it's crazy. Every now and then I re-watch "The Mother of All Demos" [1] from 1968 where Douglas Englebert demonstrates some of the research at Stanford or the Sketchpad Demo [2] from 1963 where Ivan Sutherland is presenting a GUI-based CAD system. Fortunately, these ideas have now been picked up again, but to me it's interesting to note just how long a time lapsed between these ideas and becoming mainstream. Some of it is obviously the cost as the state-of-the-art research machines were massively more powerful than the home computers even 2 decades later, but I'm sure there were a lot of great ideas that have just been forgotten. comments.quote_zh: 我真的很怀念像“mother of all demos”那样专业又随性、自然的日子
comments.text_zh: 稍微跑个题，但我真的很讨厌现在这种风气：每个开发者 / 研究者 / 工程师都还得当演员（通常还是很尬的那种），在镜头前装出古怪有个性的样子，同时还要努力表现出对这项技术不自然的兴奋。我真的很怀念像“mother of all demos”[0] 那样专业又随性、自然的状态。你能想象那个穿高领毛衣的家伙每说一句话就来一句“但是等等！”还装作很惊讶吗？那绝对不会是同一场演示了。[0] [VIDEO]
comments.text: Slightly off-topic, but I really hate this trend that now every developer / researcher / engineer also needs to be an actor (typically cringy one) pretending to be quirky for the camera while trying to act unnaturally excited about the technology. I really miss the days of the professional casualness and naturalness of something like the "mother of all demos" [0]. Like, can you imagine the guy wearing a turtleneck and going, "but wait!" and acting surprised after every sentence? It would NOT have been the same demo. [0] [VIDEO]
